title: Two inflations, and why they disagree
tension: India does not have one inflation number, it has at least two, and they routinely tell opposite stories: one can scream while the other sleeps. CPI is what you pay at the shop; WPI is what changes hands at the wholesale gate. For decades the RBI watched the wrong one, until a 2014 decision switched the country's official inflation anchor from WPI to CPI and changed how monetary policy is run. And both numbers measure a basket frozen to old spending habits, which is why the basket itself keeps getting rebuilt.
teachingGoal: Decode the two big indices and the methodology behind them: what CPI and WPI each measure, what is inside the CPI basket and in what weights, what WPI captures that CPI does not, why the two diverge, why India switched its policy anchor from WPI to CPI in 2014, and why and how the base year and basket are periodically rebuilt. The reader should know which number to trust for what.
sectionArc: Why is there more than one inflation number? (CPI = retail prices households pay, includes services; WPI = wholesale/producer prices of goods, no services)

What is actually inside the CPI basket? (the major divisions and their weights in the current 2024 basket; food and beverages the largest at about 37%; built from the household consumption-expenditure survey)
What does WPI measure that CPI doesn't? (WPI's components: primary articles, fuel and power, manufactured products; goods only, no rent, fees or services)
Why do CPI and WPI so often disagree? (different baskets and weights; WPI swings with global commodity and fuel prices; CPI is anchored by food and services)

Right now the two are screaming in opposite directions: decode it (WPI all-commodities running near 8% while CPI sits near 1%; WPI is being driven up by fuel and power around 25%, while CPI is being held down by falling food prices; same economy, two stories, and exactly why which index you watch matters)

Which number does India actually target, and why did it switch? (the 2014 move from WPI to CPI on the Urjit Patel Committee's advice; WPI ignores services and the cost of living; the RBI now targets CPI)

How and why did the basket just get rebuilt? (the February 2026 switch from the 2012 base to the 2024 base, with food's weight falling from 45.86% to 36.75%, services rising, and e-commerce, telecom data and OTT added for the first time; WPI still on 2011-12; why an out-of-date basket distorts the number)
So which inflation should you trust? (CPI for your cost of living; WPI as an early signal from the pipeline; read both, and know what each leaves out)
mustTeach: CPI measures retail prices households pay and includes services; WPI measures wholesale goods prices and excludes services
the CPI basket is dominated by food and beverages (about 46%), with miscellaneous, housing, fuel, clothing and pan/tobacco making up the rest
WPI is split into primary articles, fuel and power, and manufactured products, and is sensitive to global commodity prices
CPI and WPI diverge because their baskets and weights differ
India switched its monetary-policy anchor from WPI to CPI in 2014 on the Urjit Patel Committee's recommendation
the index uses a base year and a fixed basket that must be periodically rebuilt as spending changes (CPI 2012, new 2024 series; WPI 2011-12)

CURRENCY (important): the current official basket is the 2024-base series, launched 12 Feb 2026. Use the 2024 weights (food and beverages 36.75%) as the CURRENT weights, and cite the old 2012 weights only to show what changed. The detailed month-by-month component inflation figures (vegetables, onion, etc.) come from the longer 2012-base series and must be framed as recent readings under the previous basket, never invented for the new base.

contextCards.fact: The Consumer Price Index measures the retail prices households actually pay and includes services like rent, school fees and healthcare; its weights come from a survey of how households spend. The Wholesale Price Index measures the prices of goods traded in bulk before they reach the consumer, and contains no services at all. Because WPI is goods-only and heavy on fuel and commodities, it swings with global prices, while CPI is anchored by food and services.
contextCards.source: MoSPI / Office of the Economic Adviser methodology (standard, uncontested)

contextCards.fact: Until 2014 the RBI watched the Wholesale Price Index as its main inflation gauge. On the recommendation of the Urjit Patel Committee, it switched its anchor to the Consumer Price Index, on the logic that monetary policy should target the inflation people actually experience: WPI excludes services (over half of GDP), is driven by volatile global commodity prices, and does not capture the cost of living (rent, fees, medical bills).
contextCards.source: Urjit Patel Committee (2014); RBI shift from WPI to CPI anchoring (verified)

contextCards.fact: An inflation index measures a fixed basket against a base year. India's CPI (Combined) is built on a 2012 base, and a new series on a 2024 base has been introduced to reflect how spending has shifted (for example towards services and away from cereals). WPI is on a 2011-12 base, revised from 2004-05. An out-of-date basket misweights the things people now buy, which is why the base year is periodically updated.
contextCards.source: MoSPI CPI base-year revision (2012; new 2024 series); WPI base 2011-12 (verified)

contextCards.fact: On 12 February 2026 India launched a new Consumer Price Index series with base year 2024 (replacing 2012), built on the Household Consumption Expenditure Survey of 2023-24. The biggest change: the weight of food and beverages fell from 45.86% to 36.75%, because Indians now spend a smaller share of their budgets on food and more on services, a textbook case of Engel's law. Housing and utilities rose to about 17.7%, transport and communication to about 12.4%, and health to about 6.1%. The basket grew from 299 to 358 items, adding e-commerce and online prices, telecom data plans and OTT streaming subscriptions for the first time, and switched to the international COICOP classification of 12 divisions instead of the old six groups. Headline inflation on the new base was 2.75% in January 2026.
contextCards.source: MoSPI / NSO, first CPI release on base 2024=100, 12 February 2026; HCES 2023-24
